narrative: The model estimated a 62.6% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means, based on the information available, it judged failure somewhat more likely than passing, and your law school application was denied on that basis. The strongest factor in this prediction was your undergraduate GPA. Although your 3.40 GPA is above the 3.23 average among accepted students, it nevertheless pushed your result toward failure in this assessment. The second most important factor was your year-three class standing. Your decile of 9 was much stronger than the accepted-student average of about 5.8, and it pushed toward passing—a clear point in your favor. The third most important factor was family income. Being from an upper-middle-income bracket, which is the most common bracket among accepted students, pushed the prediction toward failure. Gender and race were not used. To move forward, ask the admissions office for individualized human review rather than relying only on the risk score. Provide context for your undergraduate GPA, emphasize your strong year-three performance, and explain any family or work responsibilities that affected your record. Ask whether updated transcripts, letters of recommendation, or a personal statement can be considered, and whether any appeal or reconsideration process is available.
